topic: AI and the future of work
blurb: What the evidence says about AI and productivity, the skills that compound, and the big economic debate.

cards.title: How AI changes work

steps.p: Economists analyze AI's impact task by task. Few jobs consist entirely of tasks AI can do.
AI can take over a task entirely, or help a person do it faster and better.
A job heavily exposed to AI may change shape, grow, or shrink — exposure alone doesn't say which.

cards.aside: Spreadsheets automated calculation, yet the number of accountants and analysts grew.

cards.q: A 2023 study by OpenAI and University of Pennsylvania researchers estimated that about what share of US workers have at least 10% of their tasks exposed to LLMs?
cards.why: About 80%. And around 19% had at least half of their tasks exposed. Higher-wage, knowledge-work jobs were generally more exposed than manual ones.

cards.statement: A job being highly exposed to AI means it will disappear.
cards.why: False. Exposure measures which tasks AI could affect. Whether that destroys, transforms or expands a job depends on demand, regulation and how firms use it.

options: Helps a person do the task, who stays in charge
cards.why: Human plus AI. Usage studies suggest a large share of real AI use is collaborative — drafting, explaining, debugging — rather than full delegation.

cards.title: Anthropic's Economic Index found software development was the most common use of Claude.
cards.detail: Analyzing millions of anonymized conversations in early 2025, it found computer and mathematical tasks made up the largest share, followed by writing and editing.

cards.q: Why do economists study AI at the level of tasks rather than whole jobs?
options: Because AI affects specific tasks, and most jobs mix exposed and unexposed tasks
cards.why: Precision. A radiologist reads scans, but also consults, decides and communicates. AI changes some of those far more than others.

cards.title: Real studies, mixed results

steps.p: A study of 5,000 agents found an AI assistant raised productivity 14% on average — and 34% for the least experienced.
In a BCG experiment, consultants using GPT-4 did much better on tasks inside AI's abilities, but worse on a task just outside them.
A 2025 METR trial found experienced open-source developers were slower with AI tools on their own projects — though they believed they were faster.

cards.aside: The lesson: AI's benefit depends heavily on the task and the person.

cards.q: In the customer support study, who gained the most from AI assistance?
cards.why: Novices, up 34%. The AI spread top performers' best practices to newer agents. The most skilled saw little benefit.

cards.statement: In METR's 2025 study, experienced open-source developers completed tasks faster when using AI tools.
cards.why: False. They took about 19% longer, despite predicting a 24% speedup and still believing afterwards that AI had made them faster. Perceived productivity can mislead.

options: Excels at some tasks and fails at others that seem equally hard, so using it outside its abilities backfires
Has rough edges in its interface
cards.why: Uneven abilities. In the BCG study, consultants on a task outside the frontier were about 19 percentage points less likely to get the right answer when using AI.

cards.title: Consultants using GPT-4 on suitable tasks finished 12% more tasks, 25% faster, with 40% higher quality.
cards.detail: The 2023 Harvard–BCG study of 758 consultants found the biggest gains among below-average performers, echoing the customer support results.

cards.title: Measure your own productivity
cards.body: People are poor judges of whether AI saves them time. Timing a real task with and without it beats any impression.
cards.challenge: Today, time one task done with AI and one similar task without, then compare honestly.

cards.title: What becomes more valuable

steps.p: When producing a draft is cheap, knowing which draft is good becomes the scarce skill.
Catching plausible-but-wrong output requires real expertise in the subject.
Deciding what to ask for — and explaining context clearly — determines what AI can deliver.

cards.aside: Expertise doesn't become worthless; it becomes the thing that makes AI useful.

cards.q: Why does verification become a more important skill as AI spreads?
options: AI output often looks convincing even when wrong, and spotting errors takes expertise
cards.why: Plausibility isn't correctness. The better AI writes, the harder errors are to notice — unless you know the subject well.

cards.title: Doctors who routinely used AI to spot growths during colonoscopies got worse at spotting them without it.
cards.detail: A 2025 study in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology found endoscopists' detection rate without AI fell from about 28% to 22% after months of AI-assisted procedures — evidence of deskilling.

cards.statement: Relying heavily on AI for a task can weaken your own ability to do it.
cards.why: True. Skills you stop practicing fade. Studies of medicine and surveys of knowledge workers suggest heavy reliance can reduce independent ability and critical thinking.

cards.q: What is the most effective way to learn a new skill with AI's help?
options: Have AI do the work for you
Attempt it yourself first, then use AI to explain, check and quiz you
Copy AI answers to memorize them
cards.why: Struggle first, then get feedback. Effortful retrieval builds memory. AI is most useful as a tutor checking your work, not a ghostwriter.

cards.statement: Trying to answer a question before seeing the answer improves learning, even if your attempt is wrong.
cards.why: True — the pretesting effect. Attempting first primes your memory to hold the correct answer. It is exactly why these lessons quiz you before explaining.

cards.title: The economic debate

steps.p: MIT economist Daron Acemoglu estimated in 2024 that AI might add only about 0.7% to total productivity over a decade.
Goldman Sachs projected in 2023 that generative AI could raise global GDP by 7% over ten years.
Past technologies destroyed some jobs but created new kinds of work that were hard to imagine beforehand.

cards.aside: The honest answer is that nobody knows yet — which is why tracking real evidence matters.

cards.q: Research by David Autor and colleagues found about what share of US workers in 2018 had job titles that didn't exist in 1940?
cards.why: About 60%. New technologies keep creating new occupations, though which jobs appear, and who gets them, is hard to predict.

cards.statement: Economists broadly agree on how much AI will increase economic growth.
cards.why: False. Estimates range from under 1% extra productivity over a decade to transformative growth. The disagreement reflects real uncertainty about adoption and capability.

cards.q: Goldman Sachs' 2023 report estimated generative AI could raise global GDP by about…
cards.why: About 7% over ten years. It also estimated work equivalent to 300 million full-time jobs was exposed to automation.

cards.title: Acemoglu's modest forecast assumed AI would profitably affect only about 5% of all tasks within a decade.
cards.detail: His argument: many exposed tasks will not be worth automating soon, and gains on hard tasks are smaller. Critics say he underestimates how fast capabilities improve.

cards.title: You finished the course — teach one thing
cards.body: Explaining something to another person is the fastest way to find out whether you really understand it, and it locks it into memory.
cards.challenge: Pick the most surprising thing you learned this month and explain it to someone today.
